common_name: Cebenese Cobweb Houseleek (Cévennes-Region Hens and Chicks)

planting.note: Press rooted offsets onto the surface of lean, gritty, fast-draining soil in spring or fall; this cobweb houseleek selection, named for France's Cévennes region, forms especially small, tight rosettes suited to trough and crevice planting.

directions: Plant in lean, mineral, sharply drained soil in full sun, where this compact cobweb houseleek selection develops its characteristic dense webbing of fine white hairs stretched across the tips of pale green, pink-edged leaves. Rosettes stay small, rarely exceeding 3 inches across, and multiply steadily by offsets to form a tight, spreading mat well suited to troughs, crevice gardens, and rock wall pockets. In summer a mother rosette sends up a short, leafy stalk of star-shaped pink flowers before dying back, leaving behind the many offsets it produced to carry the clump forward. Keep the webbing dry and the soil on the lean side, since excess moisture and rich soil both weaken the cobwebbing effect and invite rot.

common_name: Frost and Flame Hens and Chicks (Vaughn Hybrid Large Rosette Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press rooted offsets onto lean, fast-draining gritty soil in spring or fall; this large hybrid cultivar from American hybridizer Kevin Vaughn produces vigorous clumps on short stolons.

directions: Grow in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun, where this large American-bred hens and chicks cultivar develops blue-green rosettes up to 9 inches across edged in a frosting of red at the leaf tips, shifting through silvery blue, dusty pink, and deep plum tones across the seasons. Fine cilia line the leaf margins and rippled waxy watermarks pattern the surface, adding texture beyond the color display. Plants produce abundant offsets on short stolons, quickly building into a dense, impressive clump. As with all sempervivum, protect from standing winter wet rather than cold, which it shrugs off readily under a blanket of snow. NEEDS_VERIFICATION: exact registration year and parent cultivar are reported inconsistently across retail sources.

common_name: Lime Frost Hens and Chicks (Vaughn Hybrid Maroon-Edged Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press rooted offsets onto lean, fast-draining gritty soil in spring or fall; this small Vaughn hybrid forms very tight clumps on unusually short stolons.

directions: Plant in lean, mineral, sharply drained soil in full sun. This compact American-bred hybrid forms small, upright, lime-green rosettes under 3 inches tall with a striking border of deep red to maroon along each leaf margin. New offsets emerge on very short stolons, so the clump tightens quickly into a dense mound reminiscent of Jovibarba heuffelii rather than the more loosely spreading habit typical of many sempervivum. Pink summer flowers appear on a leafy stalk from a mature rosette, which then dies back as usual, leaving the clump of offsets to continue. Hardy well into winter under snow cover; the main threat is prolonged wet soil rather than cold.

common_name: Jungle Fires Hens and Chicks (Mulberry-Centered Vaughn Hybrid Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press rooted offsets onto lean, fast-draining gritty soil in spring or fall; registered by hybridizer Kevin Vaughn in the mid-1970s from a cross involving Skrocki breeding lines.

directions: Grow in lean, gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun to bring out the strong two-tone coloring of this low, open-rosetted hybrid: leaves sharply tipped in green with a glowing mulberry-red center that holds its intensity better through the growing season than many color-changing sempervivum cultivars. Rosettes spread to around 8 inches wide and multiply by offsets into a colorful, long-lived mat. Like other hardy houseleeks it tolerates extreme cold without protection, provided the soil drains quickly and does not stay saturated over winter. NEEDS_VERIFICATION: the 'Skrocki #51' parent referenced in some retail listings could not be independently confirmed beyond nursery marketing copy.

common_name: Woolcott's Variety Hens and Chicks (Red-Purple Mat-Forming Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press rooted offsets onto lean, fast-draining gritty soil in spring or fall; an older named cultivar long grown in British and American rock gardens.

directions: Plant in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun, where this long-grown cultivar forms a spreading mat of open rosettes in shifting shades of pink, silvery green, and dark red-purple, the purple tones intensifying in cool fall and winter weather. Upright flowering stems topped with pale pink, star-shaped blooms appear in summer from mature rosettes, which die back afterward as is typical of the genus, while the surrounding offsets continue spreading the clump. It is an easy, reliable rock garden and trough plant requiring only sharp drainage and full sun to perform well, tolerating poor soil and extended drought once established.

common_name: Apache Heuffelii Hens and Chicks (Burgundy-Tipped Clumping Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press rooted offsets onto lean, fast-draining gritty soil in spring or fall; heuffelii-type sempervivum clump tightly rather than spreading on long stolons, so established clumps can be lifted and divided rather than relying on loose offsets.

directions: Grow in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun. Apache forms a dense, slowly expanding clump of rosettes typical of the heuffelii group, which increase by splitting the mother rosette into new crowns rather than by producing offsets on runners. Leaves show a bright green base deepening to a rich burgundy at the tips, with the whole rosette flushing fully purple-red once cold weather sets in and fading again in spring. Like other heuffelii selections it is extremely frost hardy and drought tolerant, needing only sharp drainage to thrive, and the tight clumping habit makes it well suited to trough gardens and rock crevices where spreading sempervivum would overrun their neighbors.

common_name: Marchant's Best Red Sedum (AGM Reddish-Pink Upright Stonecrop)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; bred by Graham Gough of Marchant's Hardy Plants in the UK and given the RHS Award of Garden Merit in 2006.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun. This erect, clump-forming stonecrop carries yellow-green foliage strongly flushed with red that deepens further in bright sun, held on sturdy dark red stems that resist flopping. Tightly structured flower clusters open from grey-green buds into a strong reddish pink in late summer, and the spent flower and seed heads weather to a dark reddish brown that remains attractive through winter frost and snow. Leave the old stems standing through the cold season for structure and shelter for beneficial insects, cutting back to new growth in early spring. Divide congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Minor Dwarf Jade Plant (Compact Bushy Jade Cultivar)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Minor stays markedly smaller and denser than the standard jade plant.

directions: Grow in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix, letting the soil dry out fully between waterings. Minor is a compact jade plant cultivar with small, glossy, densely packed leaves and a slightly irregular, twiggy branching habit that gives older specimens a dwarfed, tree-like silhouette well suited to bonsai-style training. Leaf tips take on a red blush under strong light or cool conditions, echoing the color response of the species. Small white flowers can appear in winter on well-established plants. As with other jade plant cultivars, propagate easily from leaf or stem cuttings allowed to callus briefly before rooting in dry succulent mix.

common_name: Fleur Blanc Echeveria (Icy Blue Rosette with Coral Bells)

planting.note: Plant offsets or container stock in spring in well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun to part shade; Fleur Blanc requires perfect drainage and is intolerant of standing water in the center of the rosette.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, gritty to sandy soil in full sun to part shade. Fleur Blanc forms a pastel, icy-blue rosette of broad, rounded leaves that blush pink-purple near the tips in strong light and cool conditions. Arching flower stalks carry bell-shaped blooms in a coral-to-golden-yellow shade with purple-pink undertones on the reverse, a contrast with the frosty blue foliage that makes it a popular display plant. Like other echeveria it needs sharp drainage and infrequent, deep watering, with the soil allowed to dry out fully between waterings. In zone 9 protect from prolonged winter wet and hard freezes, bringing containers under cover if frost threatens.

planting.note: Plant offsets or container stock in spring in well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun; a Japanese-named selection of the painted echeveria grown for its bold raised markings.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun, allowing the soil to dry between waterings. This selection of the painted echeveria forms a solitary central rosette marked with irregular splashes of crimson-red and raised, bumpy caruncles (small wart-like growths) scattered across the upper leaf surface, a trait shared with the straight species but more pronounced here. Growth is slow and the rosette stays fairly compact, rarely offsetting heavily, which makes it a good specimen plant for a single container or a prominent rock garden pocket. Pinkish-white, bell-shaped flowers appear on arching stalks in fall. It will not tolerate a hard frost and should be moved under cover or grown in a container that can be brought indoors where winters bring freezing temperatures.

common_name: Super Clone Zebra Plant (Extra-Large Banded Haworthiopsis Cultivar)

planting.note: Divide offsets in spring and pot in a shallow container with fast-draining succulent mix; Super Clone is a selected zebra haworthia form roughly twice the size of the commonly grown species.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light or part sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix, watering only once the soil has dried out. This selected clone of the familiar zebra haworthia is roughly twice the size of the common form, producing a cluster of nearly stemless rosettes of firm, triangular leaves covered in raised white tubercles arranged in distinct horizontal bands on the leaf undersides. In late winter and spring, slender flowering stalks rise well above the foliage, carrying small white flowers striped in greenish pink. It is slow growing and very long-lived, clumping steadily over many years to form a dense mound well suited to containers, rock gardens in frost-free climates, or a bright windowsill.

common_name: Spider White Fairy Washboard (Heavily White-Marked Limifolia Cultivar)

planting.note: Divide offsets in spring and pot in a shallow container with fast-draining succulent mix; Spider White is a heavily marked selection of the fairy washboard haworthia.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light or part shade in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix, watering only once the soil has dried out completely. Spider White is a selection of the fairy washboard haworthia grown for its exceptionally heavy, dense white tuberculate ridging, which gives the spiraling, triangular leaves a stark, frosted appearance against the dark green leaf base, far more pronounced than on typical species plants. The tight, low rosettes clump readily by offsets, forming a compact mound well suited to shallow dish gardens and windowsill collections. Avoid direct hot sun, which can scorch the leaves, and protect from frost, since it is hardy only in essentially frost-free climates outdoors.

common_name: Purple Delight Graptopetalum (Frosty Lilac-Pink Hybrid Rosette)

planting.note: Root offsets or stem cuttings in spring in lean, gritty succulent mix; a hybrid of Graptopetalum amethystinum and G. paraguayense that branches at the base with age.

directions: Grow in lean, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light, watering only once the soil has dried out completely. This hybrid between Graptopetalum amethystinum and G. paraguayense produces pale, frost-bloomed leaves in rosettes at the ends of slender stems, shifting from deep lilac and pink-red to a frosty near-white depending on light intensity and season. Star-shaped white flowers with scattered red dots open in spring on simple stalks near the stem tips. It branches at the base as it matures, eventually forming a small clustered mound, and roots readily from leaf or stem cuttings. NEEDS_VERIFICATION: some retail sources treat 'Purple Delight' as a synonym of Graptopetalum 'Snow White' rather than a distinct cultivar; this record covers the plant sold under the 'Purple Delight' name.

common_name: Blue Haze Pachyphytum (Lavender-Blue Hybrid Bead Succulent)

planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix; a nursery hybrid between Pachyphytum bracteosum and P. glutinicaule.

directions: Plant in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in full sun to bright light, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings. This hybrid between Pachyphytum bracteosum and P. glutinicaule carries plump, chunky leaves in soft pastel shades of lavender and powder blue, with a moderate farina coating that intensifies the color under strong light. Rosettes clump slowly by basal offsets, staying low and compact rather than trailing. Handle plants carefully and avoid wetting the foliage directly, since the powdery surface bloom marks easily and does not regenerate once rubbed off. Propagate by rooting individual leaves or short stem cuttings in dry succulent mix.
